THE BIG PLAN

By: Joy Summers | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Covid19 gives us an opportunity to reimagine our future. The country faces a stark choice and the actions taken by leaders in the immediate future will set the country on one of two paths, so says one

Unique Selling Point:
Entrepreneurs who are usually shy are so fed up they are prepared to tell it like it is.

Summary:
Covid19 gives us an opportunity to reimagine our future. The country faces a stark choice and the actions taken by leaders in the immediate future will set the country on one of two paths, so says one of two new plans for SA released in July. Which one will we choose and what are the consequences if we don’t choose wisely?

Summary
Three million jobs in three months have been lost due to Covid19. Sector by sector it’s a blood bath, GDP has declined by 30%. Debt levels are sky-rocketing and the poor are starving. What we need now more than ever are jobs and building an inclusive economy. Carte Blanche asks the ANC and business to defend their plans. Both look to mining and manufacturing to create wealth and jobs, so Carte Blanche gets onto the factory floor to see how both heavy industry, and the steel industry are doing, and finds an industry in such dire straights that they may not last long enough to be saved by anyone, and if these cornerstone industries go, they will be lost forever.


Further information:
Further information
The ANC’s plan titled reconstruction, growth and Transformation- Building a new inclusive economy envisages more state control, more state enterprises, huge infrastructure project, dipping into private pension funds, regulating the banks, and nationalizing the reserve bank.
RW Johnson has the following to say about the ANC plan.

The new ANC economic statement is a bizarre document. It repeatedly says that the pandemic has created new opportunities. With three million jobs lost and 47% of households going hungry it is clear that these “opportunities” do not apply to the people at large. Instead they are opportunities for the ANC elite to consolidate their power. Under the heading “The balance of forces” the document tells us that as a result of the pandemic:
“… the contested relationship between the public and private sectors has shifted. The pandemic has reinforced the legitimacy of public investment in health care. It has legitimized a greater and more active role of the state in guiding the economy. It has forced a rethink on public services that are now seen as a necessary investment rather than a liability. Central banks are increasingly being called upon to assume a more active and direct role in supporting the real economy.”

Others have called it hopeless, out of touch, confusing, and a case of singing the same old song. But it can’t be all bad, and we have invited the ANC head of the Economic Transformation committee to promote the ideas in his document.

Manufacturing and mining are seen as key productive sectors. It acknowledges significant de- industrialization and job losses. The plan says it wants to rebuild local manufacturing and drive import substitution. They want to rebuild the rail manufacturing capacity and manufacturing linked to the mineral beneficiation chains including steel value chains including iron- ore, manganese and chromium. All good so far but stop right there. Because our research shows that the companies that are providing these products may not be around for much longer.

THE STEEL INDUSTRY
Theunis Duvenage, Aslam Osman and Doron Friedman all have solid medium sized businesses supplying steel products. These are companies with values around R300 million rand or more – the exact kind of company the state says we need more of. So why then is Osman taking government to court, Theunis is nervous, and Doron Friedman is about to pack up his company and ship it off to Mauritius? All three blame duties about to be imposed by the state to protect Arcelor Mittal – a company owned by an Indian Billionaire and 5 politically connected shareholders that siphon off the profits, don’t reinvest and provide products that are expensive and sub- standard. These three entrepreneurs say that if they are prevented from bringing in high quality steel from China – they will go out of business or close down their businesses. But Arcelor Mittal will lose jobs you may say- they agree 1600 jobs, but if the steel manufacturing companies go out of business – 300 000 could be lost. So while the new ANC plan envisages local production at all costs – it is busy destroying what it says it wants to save. At NIASA representatives are spending 40 – 60 percent of their time on negotiating retrenchments with workers. Go figure.

THE BIG GUNS – MINING AND MINERALS
The ANC has a soft spot for these two sectors and beneficiation is high on the plans agenda.
But its magical thinking because on the ground the sector faces an imminent demise- the reason – the cost and unreliability of Eskom. It’s a factor that both plans acknowledge needs to change but will that change come soon enough, because what is happening on the ground is industrial devastation. 90% of small foundries have closed. Only one out of 22 plants at Glencore is operational in winter because the cost of electricity, SAMANCOR’S furnace never came out of lockdown. This is a sector that provides 68 000 jobs, contributed R41 billion to SA GDP and more than 2 billion dollars in foreign income and R1.5 billion in PAYE. Now Eskom is champing at the bit to raise electricity prices to double digit increases.
“It will kill off a lot of the industry” says Nic Dawson who represents the sector as part of the EIUG. Already Samancor have sent out section 189 retrenchment notices and now Glencore is doing the same. We will speak to Ferro Alloys representative Chairman Chabisi Motloung

We will speak to the players in the steel industry, Busi Mavuso and hopefully Enoch Godongwana about why their plans should be adopted and if they aren’t what fate awaits us.

THE BIG PLAN FINAL SCRIPT FOR BROADCAST TX SUNDAY 9th AUGUST 2020

Commentary One
For 97 years Robor was one of Southern Africa’s largest suppliers of steel, tube and pipe.
But the clanking of steel is gone, the racks are empty -the steel auctioned -last Friday this enormous factory closed its doors for the last time and another 900 people ended up jobless.

Our local steel industry is dying - from the downstream manufacturers to the enormous smelters that take the ore out of the ground and turn it into the alloys that are used to make steel

Heat sparks flying around

Derek
Here is something to warm your heart this winter this is alloy being smelted at nearly 1500 degrees

Commentary Two
But our heavy industry has become a twilight industry as smelters like these close down.
Last year this industry contributed forty billion rand to the fiscus, now its evaporating as the
flames are extinguished, the jobs die, and only rust and decay remain.

Chabisi Motloung is chairperson of the Ferro Alloys Producers Association.

Derek
Is this a big part of your business?
Chabisi
This is the main thing! This is the main thing! You turn a rock into this and this goes into the steel industry. The highest value add in the value chain is converting a rock into this and that step you don’t want to lose out of the country. This is the step you want to keep in the country
Derek
But it’s the step we are in danger of losing
Chabisi
This is the step that is on the verge of extinction.

Commentary Three
We have the expertise, we have the ore, but we have lost our competitive edge, and if we are looking for a culprit, try Eskom, it’s 500 % increase in seven years is crippling the ferro- alloy industry. In 2019 it paid Eskom R14 billion rand, but now Eskom wants another increase.

Derek
So, this latest increase is like another nail in the coffin.
Chabisi
It's definitely the last nail in the coffin.
Commentary Four
we need a plan urgently – and in July two economic recovery plans were released on the same day. One from Business for South Africa – the other from the ANC. The ANC plan pushes mining and local beneficiation of chrome and manganese and that is what this industry wants.

Derek Link
But even the best laid plans can go awry and what is written in the ANC plan really has no bearing on what is happening right here on the ground in heavy industry

Commentary five
These graphs show how South Africa was the worldwide hub of Chrome and manganese alloy production, only seven years ago, now all of that has been given away to China

Derek
We're exporting the raw material and then importing back the finished product
Chabisi
That is there is very well put. If I can sum it up basically, we are feeding the monster that is actually eating us alive

Commentary Six
It’s a vicious cycle that needs urgent government intervention, because to save this industry they need cheaper power, but when Chabisi and his executives knock on government doors nothing happens

Chabisi
And we did have get a lot of sympathy from all the departments that we visited. But no one is taking action.

Commentary seven
Minister Ebrahim Patel is open to speak to Carte Blanche when he recovers from the Corona virus. He says the fundamental challenge faced in the steel industry is the global overproduction of steel with significant expansion in China. He is working on a steel master plan.

But there is another plan to reimagine our future, and it comes from Business for South Africa. Business leadership was a founding member and Busi Mavuso is CEO.

Derek
You interact with big business all the time. How concerned are leaders in business?
Busi
Business confidence is currently sitting at five percent Derek, that's how concerned they are. They don't believe in the ability of South Africa to be able to deliver what it needs to deliver.



Commentary Eight
Meanwhile the deindustrialising of our foundation industries is accelerating. Molten wealth producing giants reduced to carcasses of scrap metal. But the plan from business for SA says we can reverse our decline by focusing on policy certainty, state capacity, inequality and transformation, inefficient and redundant SOE’S, education, corruption and crime

Derek
So, to be brutally honest, where are we now In South Africa?
Busi
Finance Minister Tito Mboweni said that if things don't change radically, in the next three years South Africa is going to be facing a sovereign debt crisis and that is the reality of the situation.

Commentary nine
Treasury is concerned about our debt and- we have just received our first IMF loan of R70 billion.

Busi
The feedback after we received that loan, the international market and the local market are saying that we are hoping that that money is not going to be stolen. That is what the international market thinks of South Africa. They're not thinking what are the critical interventions that have to be looked at, they are saying we are hoping that they won’t steal it, and unfortunately, I'm right there with them!

Commentary Ten
The first pillar of the ANC economic transformation plan is an infrastructure led recovery. Its second pillar says it will promote investment in agriculture, manufacturing, mining, and tourism. They also want to see more state- owned companies

Busi Mavuso
And they still harping around their state bank, the state pharmaceutical company. I would have thought that having 743 SOE’s that are all failing, you probably would give up on the idea of actually coming up with more SOE’S

Derek link
The plans don’t always agree on what must be done, where they do agree is that we are out of time and urgent steps must be taken, because it’s not a pretty picture on the factory floor

Commentary Eleven
Theunis Duvenage began selling roofing when he was still at school. Now he has a medium sized company that employs around 100 people. His is exactly the kind of company we need more of, so he is alarmed to watch other Steel manufacturers folding before his eyes

Theunis
Just last week another one went into business rescue, there are other business’s that closed down. Robor closed down



Commentary Twelve
The fight here by the downstream manufacturers is not with Eskom, but rather with Minister Patel. Ironically, they say can import better quality cheaper Chinese steel than our local steel producer Arcelor Mittal. But Patel has imposed duties on imported steel to protect Arcelor Mittal

Theunis
What is a mystery to me is that we see these job losses but still the duties start piling on, piling on..

Commentary Thirteen
He says Arcelor Mittal’s mill is 70 years old and inefficient and by protecting a single company- Arcelor Mittal, the minister puts thousands of companies and 250 000 jobs at risk

Theunis
Arcelor Mittal is run by clever business- people. I know them, so they have been asked to participate in a grand- prix but they are sitting with a 1960 beetle, its not possible for them to compete

Commentary fourteen
Kobus Verster is the CEO of Arcelor Mittal. He rejects the allegations that their technology is old, and their steel is too expensive.

Kobus
Our price of steel is governed by an agreement with government, and that's the only price we can charge. Would I like to push up prices now? Yes, I would like to do it. I can't

Commentary Fifteen
Now there are more duties coming and that will be the death knell for the downstream industry according to a court application for an interdict this week by NEASA, the National Employers association led by Gerhard Papenfuss.

Gerhard
Governments actions have prejudiced this industry for years and it has caused deindustrialization. The only answer is jobs and for that you need business that prosper and they can’t prosper if they don’t compete

Commentary Sixteen
Doron Friedman’s company makes the frames for dry walling, and he has been fighting the duties since 2015.

Derek
Okay. What is on the table right now what is really concerning.
Dorond
Well what's concerning me is that If ArcelorMittal are successful the downstream will die. And the only way I can survive, I would have to take my jobs that I'm creating here and move them somewhere else. And that was one of the reasons why I've set up a company in Mauritius
Derek
But you are ready to pull the trigger and move out of the country.
Doron
If I can't make money in South Africa because I'm not competitive. Do I have a choice I have to pull the trigger?

Commentary seventeen
Verster is unapologetic about the duties Arcelor Mittal needs to survive

KOBUS
The duty is there to create fairness. The Chinese mills have the cheapest labour in the world. They get incentives to export to other countries. Their electricity is the cheapest in the world, ours is the most expensive our rail tariffs are the most expensive. So how do you equalize that. You do it through tariffs. That's what other countries in the world do.

Commentary Eighteen
Minister Patel says that although tariff protection does seek to balance the competing needs of the industry on its own its not sufficient to deal with the challenge and that they are developing a plan to support jobs and downstream growth

Kobus
The steel part of the economy has been shrinking for the last ten years

Commentary Nineteen
One thing both the ANC and Business plan agree on is expanding infrastructure, but will that be enough to revive our steel industry? These are questions we had for the ANC’s Enoch Godongwana, but he chose not to speak to Carte Blanche

Busi Mavuso
I think one of our epic failures is until we are decisive, and we are clear, whether this country is led by the state or whether it's led by the party, we are actually not going to make any progress
Derek
But Busi our president is a businessman the very astute businessman. Does he not have the powers to implement what he would like to see in the country?
Busi
If you want to turn a country like South Africa around, I think just accept that when all your interventions are said and done, you are not going to be loved by everyone. But that's key because this is not a popularity contest, right?! You don't do this because you…. you're doing it because you know that 59 million South Africans have said that Mr. President we would like you to deliver a better life for all, not a million ANC voters- 59 million South Africans and I think that is lost on him.

Commentary Twenty
Late in July the president announced that R340 billion rand would be spent on strategic infrastructure projects.

Derek:
A few hours after this plan was released the ANC put forward their own plan, they're in charge, so wont they ignore this plan
Busi:
Let me say there's some alignment between our plan and the plan that is put together /but I guess where the ANC probably maybe speaks from both sides of their mouths- and my view is you talk about policy certainty and then you talk about prescribed assets in the form of amending Regulation 28 eight and saying that I'm gonna be taking your pension money you know to be able to advance or implement the infrastructure project

Commentary Twenty- One
The business for South Africa plan is detailed. 250 industry experts worked free for four months to put it together. It says we can add R1 trillion rand to our GDP if we implement it. Both plans are on our website.

Derek
The big question is: has the government, the ANC taken an interest in this plan?
Busi
We have an engagement with government - taken an interest I'm not sure. I don't think so, because there was actually a very specific request to see that can we have a…I think was set for a side or six aside to look at the plan and see how we can start implementing it
Derek
Combine the two maybe and take the best elements from each plan?
Busi
And we still haven't moved on that, so have they jumped on it? No, to them its just yet another plan.

Commentary Twenty- Two
This week the CEO of the Black business council Kganki Matabane, voiced his frustration. We are always announcing plans he said. There is no action that follows the words. And no action means 15 000 direct and another 100 000 indirect jobs will be lost within two years by the smelters. And even more, if the steel manufacturers close up shop.

And once factories close, they never come back.

THE END DURATION 13: 59

PROMO ONE
The national mood is bleak, as companies close and jobs are lost. Now we have two new plans to reimagine our future one from Business the other from the ANC.



PROMO TWO
Big industry is in crisis, but an ANC economic transformation plan wants to revive it. But does their plan have any bearing on what is happening on the ground.


PROMO THREE
250 specialists volunteered their time to put together a recovery plan for Business for South Africa. But is government interested in what they have to say.

The ANC plan pushes mining and local beneficiation of chrome and manganese and that is what this industry wants. Derek Link But even the best laid plans can go awry and what is written in the ANC plan really has no bearing on what is happening right here on the ground in heavy industry Commentary five These graphs show how South Africa was the worldwide hub of Chrome and manganese alloy production, only seven years ago, now all of that has been given away to China Derek We're exporting the raw material and then importing back the finished product Chabisi That is there is very well put. If I can sum it up basically, we are feeding the monster that is actually eating us alive Commentary Six It’s a vicious cycle that needs urgent government intervention, because to save this industry they need cheaper power, but when Chabisi and his executives knock on government doors nothing happens Chabisi And we did have get a lot of sympathy from all the departments that we visited. But no one is taking action. Commentary seven Minister Ebrahim Patel is open to speak to Carte Blanche when he recovers from the Corona virus. He says the fundamental challenge faced in the steel industry is the global overproduction of steel with significant expansion in China. He is working on a steel master plan. But there is another plan to reimagine our future, and it comes from Business for South Africa. Business leadership was a founding member and Busi Mavuso is CEO. Derek You interact with big business all the time. How concerned are leaders in business? Busi Business confidence is currently sitting at five percent Derek, that's how concerned they are. They don't believe in the ability of South Africa to be able to deliver what it needs to deliver. Commentary Eight Meanwhile the deindustrialising of our foundation industries is accelerating. Molten wealth producing giants reduced to carcasses of scrap metal. But the plan from business for SA says we can reverse our decline by focusing on policy certainty, state capacity, inequality and transformation, inefficient and redundant SOE’S, education, corruption and crime Derek So, to be brutally honest, where are we now In South Africa? Busi Finance Minister Tito Mboweni said that if things don't change radically, in the next three years South Africa is going to be facing a sovereign debt crisis and that is the reality of the situation. Commentary nine Treasury is concerned about our debt and- we have just received our first IMF loan of R70 billion. Busi The feedback after we received that loan, the international market and the local market are saying that we are hoping that that money is not going to be stolen. That is what the international market thinks of South Africa. They're not thinking what are the critical interventions that have to be looked at, they are saying we are hoping that they won’t steal it, and unfortunately, I'm right there with them! Commentary Ten The first pillar of the ANC economic transformation plan is an infrastructure led recovery. Its second pillar says it will promote investment in agriculture, manufacturing, mining, and tourism. They also want to see more state- owned companies Busi Mavuso And they still harping around their state bank, the state pharmaceutical company. I would have thought that having 743 SOE’s that are all failing, you probably would give up on the idea of actually coming up with more SOE’S Derek link The plans don’t always agree on what must be done, where they do agree is that we are out of time and urgent steps must be taken, because it’s not a pretty picture on the factory floor Commentary Eleven Theunis Duvenage began selling roofing when he was still at school. Now he has a medium sized company that employs around 100 people. His is exactly the kind of company we need more of, so he is alarmed to watch other Steel manufacturers folding before his eyes Theunis Just last week another one went into business rescue, there are other business’s that closed down. Robor closed down Commentary Twelve The fight here by the downstream manufacturers is not with Eskom, but rather with Minister Patel. Ironically, they say can import better quality cheaper Chinese steel than our local steel producer Arcelor Mittal. But Patel has imposed duties on imported steel to protect Arcelor Mittal Theunis What is a mystery to me is that we see these job losses but still the duties start piling on, piling on.. Commentary Thirteen He says Arcelor Mittal’s mill is 70 years old and inefficient and by protecting a single company- Arcelor Mittal, the minister puts thousands of companies and 250 000 jobs at risk Theunis Arcelor Mittal is run by clever business- people. I know them, so they have been asked to participate in a grand- prix but they are sitting with a 1960 beetle, its not possible for them to compete Commentary fourteen Kobus Verster is the CEO of Arcelor Mittal. He rejects the allegations that their technology is old, and their steel is too expensive. Kobus Our price of steel is governed by an agreement with government, and that's the only price we can charge. Would I like to push up prices now? Yes, I would like to do it. I can't Commentary Fifteen Now there are more duties coming and that will be the death knell for the downstream industry according to a court application for an interdict this week by NEASA, the National Employers association led by Gerhard Papenfuss. Gerhard Governments actions have prejudiced this industry for years and it has caused deindustrialization. The only answer is jobs and for that you need business that prosper and they can’t prosper if they don’t compete Commentary Sixteen Doron Friedman’s company makes the frames for dry walling, and he has been fighting the duties since 2015. Derek Okay. What is on the table right now what is really concerning. Dorond Well what's concerning me is that If ArcelorMittal are successful the downstream will die. And the only way I can survive, I would have to take my jobs that I'm creating here and move them somewhere else. And that was one of the reasons why I've set up a company in Mauritius Derek But you are ready to pull the trigger and move out of the country. Doron If I can't make money in South Africa because I'm not competitive. Do I have a choice I have to pull the trigger? Commentary seventeen Verster is unapologetic about the duties Arcelor Mittal needs to survive KOBUS The duty is there to create fairness. The Chinese mills have the cheapest labour in the world. They get incentives to export to other countries. Their electricity is the cheapest in the world, ours is the most expensive our rail tariffs are the most expensive. So how do you equalize that. You do it through tariffs. That's what other countries in the world do. Commentary Eighteen Minister Patel says that although tariff protection does seek to balance the competing needs of the industry on its own its not sufficient to deal with the challenge and that they are developing a plan to support jobs and downstream growth Kobus The steel part of the economy has been shrinking for the last ten years Commentary Nineteen One thing both the ANC and Business plan agree on is expanding infrastructure, but will that be enough to revive our steel industry? These are questions we had for the ANC’s Enoch Godongwana, but he chose not to speak to Carte Blanche Busi Mavuso I think one of our epic failures is until we are decisive, and we are clear, whether this country is led by the state or whether it's led by the party, we are actually not going to make any progress Derek But Busi our president is a businessman the very astute businessman. Does he not have the powers to implement what he would like to see in the country? Busi If you want to turn a country like South Africa around, I think just accept that when all your interventions are said and done, you are not going to be loved by everyone. But that's key because this is not a popularity contest, right?! You don't do this because you…. you're doing it because you know that 59 million South Africans have said that Mr. President we would like you to deliver a better life for all, not a million ANC voters- 59 million South Africans and I think that is lost on him. Commentary Twenty Late in July the president announced that R340 billion rand would be spent on strategic infrastructure projects. Derek: A few hours after this plan was released the ANC put forward their own plan, they're in charge, so wont they ignore this plan Busi: Let me say there's some alignment between our plan and the plan that is put together /but I guess where the ANC probably maybe speaks from both sides of their mouths- and my view is you talk about policy certainty and then you talk about prescribed assets in the form of amending Regulation 28 eight and saying that I'm gonna be taking your pension money you know to be able to advance or implement the infrastructure project Commentary Twenty- One The business for South Africa plan is detailed. 250 industry experts worked free for four months to put it together. It says we can add R1 trillion rand to our GDP if we implement it. Both plans are on our website. Derek The big question is: has the government, the ANC taken an interest in this plan? Busi We have an engagement with government - taken an interest I'm not sure. I don't think so, because there was actually a very specific request to see that can we have a…I think was set for a side or six aside to look at the plan and see how we can start implementing it Derek Combine the two maybe and take the best elements from each plan? Busi And we still haven't moved on that, so have they jumped on it? No, to them its just yet another plan. Commentary Twenty- Two This week the CEO of the Black business council Kganki Matabane, voiced his frustration. We are always announcing plans he said. There is no action that follows the words. And no action means 15 000 direct and another 100 000 indirect jobs will be lost within two years by the smelters. And even more, if the steel manufacturers close up shop. And once factories close, they never come back. THE END DURATION 13: 59 PROMO ONE The national mood is bleak, as companies close and jobs are lost. Now we have two new plans to reimagine our future one from Business the other from the ANC. PROMO TWO Big industry is in crisis, but an ANC economic transformation plan wants to revive it. But does their plan have any bearing on what is happening on the ground. PROMO THREE 250 specialists volunteered their time to put together a recovery plan for Business for South Africa. But is government interested in what they have to say. Invoicing Back references from Insert ID in Invoice: Title Author Last Updated Invoice for THE BIG PLAN (5733) Joy Summers 13 August 2020

metadata.Summary: Covid19 gives us an opportunity to reimagine our future. The country faces a stark choice and the actions taken by leaders in the immediate future will set the country on one of two paths, so says one of two new plans for SA released in July. Which one will we choose and what are the consequences if we don’t choose wisely? Summary Three million jobs in three months have been lost due to Covid19. Sector by sector it’s a blood bath, GDP has declined by 30%. Debt levels are sky-rocketing and the poor are starving. What we need now more than ever are jobs and building an inclusive economy. Carte Blanche asks the ANC and business to defend their plans. Both look to mining and manufacturing to create wealth and jobs, so Carte Blanche gets onto the factory floor to see how both heavy industry, and the steel industry are doing, and finds an industry in such dire straights that they may not last long enough to be saved by anyone, and if these cornerstone industries go, they will be lost forever.
metadata.Further information: Further information The ANC’s plan titled reconstruction, growth and Transformation- Building a new inclusive economy envisages more state control, more state enterprises, huge infrastructure project, dipping into private pension funds, regulating the banks, and nationalizing the reserve bank. RW Johnson has the following to say about the ANC plan. The new ANC economic statement is a bizarre document. It repeatedly says that the pandemic has created new opportunities. With three million jobs lost and 47% of households going hungry it is clear that these “opportunities” do not apply to the people at large. Instead they are opportunities for the ANC elite to consolidate their power. Under the heading “The balance of forces” the document tells us that as a result of the pandemic: “… the contested relationship between the public and private sectors has shifted. The pandemic has reinforced the legitimacy of public investment in health care. It has legitimized a greater and more active role of the state in guiding the economy. It has forced a rethink on public services that are now seen as a necessary investment rather than a liability. Central banks are increasingly being called upon to assume a more active and direct role in supporting the real economy.” Others have called it hopeless, out of touch, confusing, and a case of singing the same old song. But it can’t be all bad, and we have invited the ANC head of the Economic Transformation committee to promote the ideas in his document. Manufacturing and mining are seen as key productive sectors. It acknowledges significant de- industrialization and job losses. The plan says it wants to rebuild local manufacturing and drive import substitution. They want to rebuild the rail manufacturing capacity and manufacturing linked to the mineral beneficiation chains including steel value chains including iron- ore, manganese and chromium. All good so far but stop right there. Because our research shows that the companies that are providing these products may not be around for much longer. THE STEEL INDUSTRY Theunis Duvenage, Aslam Osman and Doron Friedman all have solid medium sized businesses supplying steel products. These are companies with values around R300 million rand or more – the exact kind of company the state says we need more of. So why then is Osman taking government to court, Theunis is nervous, and Doron Friedman is about to pack up his company and ship it off to Mauritius? All three blame duties about to be imposed by the state to protect Arcelor Mittal – a company owned by an Indian Billionaire and 5 politically connected shareholders that siphon off the profits, don’t reinvest and provide products that are expensive and sub- standard. These three entrepreneurs say that if they are prevented from bringing in high quality steel from China – they will go out of business or close down their businesses. But Arcelor Mittal will lose jobs you may say- they agree 1600 jobs, but if the steel manufacturing companies go out of business – 300 000 could be lost. So while the new ANC plan envisages local production at all costs – it is busy destroying what it says it wants to save. At NIASA representatives are spending 40 – 60 percent of their time on negotiating retrenchments with workers. Go figure. THE BIG GUNS – MINING AND MINERALS The ANC has a soft spot for these two sectors and beneficiation is high on the plans agenda. But its magical thinking because on the ground the sector faces an imminent demise- the reason – the cost and unreliability of Eskom. It’s a factor that both plans acknowledge needs to change but will that change come soon enough, because what is happening on the ground is industrial devastation. 90% of small foundries have closed. Only one out of 22 plants at Glencore is operational in winter because the cost of electricity, SAMANCOR’S furnace never came out of lockdown. This is a sector that provides 68 000 jobs, contributed R41 billion to SA GDP and more than 2 billion dollars in foreign income and R1.5 billion in PAYE. Now Eskom is champing at the bit to raise electricity prices to double digit increases. “It will kill off a lot of the industry” says Nic Dawson who represents the sector as part of the EIUG. Already Samancor have sent out section 189 retrenchment notices and now Glencore is doing the same. We will speak to Ferro Alloys representative Chairman Chabisi Motloung We will speak to the players in the steel industry, Busi Mavuso and hopefully Enoch Godongwana about why their plans should be adopted and if they aren’t what fate awaits us.
